whyCorrect: The colon explains the blank: True History contains space travel and interplanetary conflict, and some scholars call it the earliest work of science fiction. A second-century text anticipating a genre that appears much later is forward-looking, which is what visionary means. The "however" also signals it stands apart from Lucian's usual critiques of philosophers.

whyWrong.A: Means officially permitted, which has nothing to do with anticipating a genre.
whyWrong.B: Means relevant to a particular case, but the sentence is about the work being ahead of its time, not about applicability.
whyWrong.C: Describes a tone of mockery — plausible for a satirist, but the colon explains the blank in terms of science fiction tropes, not tone, and "however" marks this work as unlike his usual satire.

tips: When a colon follows the blank, the material after it defines the word — do not choose on the basis of the writer's general reputation.

whyCorrect: The sentence says the tenrecs are "not closely related" to hedgehogs yet possess spines, pointed snouts, and small size — the same traits — which the two groups developed independently. The blank names what they share, so it needs a word for resemblances plus the preposition that links them to hedgehogs: similarities with.

whyWrong.A: Would make the traits examples of true hedgehogs, but tenrecs are not hedgehogs and the sentence says so.
whyWrong.B: Attributes worries to animals, which the list of physical traits does not support.
whyWrong.C: Would mean the traits are signs pointing to true hedgehogs, whereas the text says the two groups evolved them separately.

tips: Check the preposition as well as the noun — a word can be right in meaning and still fail because it takes the wrong preposition here.

whyCorrect: Richter's sentence spells out the problem: "new batteries can't be put in once the old ones no longer work." Putting in a new battery for a dead one is replacing it, so the blank must be replaced. The consequence — devices stop working and get thrown out — follows from exactly that.

whyWrong.A: Means assigned a rating; a battery's rating has no bearing on whether the device becomes trash.
whyWrong.B: Means created for the first time, but these batteries already exist inside the devices.
whyWrong.C: Means stopped from happening, which cannot take a physical battery as its object here.

commonMistakes: Choosing a word that sounds technical about batteries instead of the one the following sentence literally paraphrases.

whyCorrect: The text opens by inviting you to assume the answer is no, then overturns that assumption: seeds of many common species germinated in simulated Martian soil, and field mustard did better there — 30 percent versus 4 percent — than in Earth soil. The setup exists to make the result land as a surprise, so the purpose is to present that surprising finding.

whyWrong.A: How the soil was simulated is never explained; the simulated soil is the setting for the experiment, not its subject.
whyWrong.C: Water appears only as a stated condition ("as long as water is supplied"), and no unexpected result about water is reported.
whyWrong.D: The chemical composition of the two soils is never compared — the text compares germination rates.

tips: When a passage opens with a question and a "you might think," the purpose is almost always to overturn the expected answer.

whyCorrect: The text gives two reasons scholars care about juvenilia. Work by writers who became famous, like Dickens's early poem, shows how those authors developed; and work by lesser-known writers, like Ashford's widely read novels, matters for understanding literary history. Both halves are about why the material is worth studying.

whyWrong.A: Publication difficulties are never mentioned; Dickens's poem is described as unpublished, but no struggle to publish is discussed.
whyWrong.C: The text compares two kinds of juvenilia scholarship, not young writers against adult contemporaries.
whyWrong.D: Ashford and Dickens are used to illustrate two reasons for interest, and no judgment ranks their literary merit.

commonMistakes: Latching onto the "But" and treating the second reason as a rebuttal, when both reasons are being presented as valid.

whyCorrect: Both examples take the same route. Cocoa went from Nahuatl to Spanish to English, and puma went from Quechua to Spanish to English. Spanish is the shared middle step in each chain, so the point being made about it is that it carried Indigenous words into English.

whyWrong.B: No quantities of vocabulary are compared anywhere in the text.
whyWrong.C: Two words are traced, one from each language, which establishes nothing about how many words Spanish adopted from either.
whyWrong.D: Spanish is only shown borrowing from Indigenous languages; the text never says it gave words back to them.

tips: When two examples follow the same three-step path, the question is usually about the step they have in common.

whyCorrect: The sentence beginning "But" isolates what is distinctive: Drelichman and Voth reconstructed the earliest surviving annual fiscal records for any sovereign state, and those records show Philip's defaults came from short-term liquidity crises rather than long-term unsustainable debt. That is new evidence doing two things at once — ruling out one explanation and establishing the other.

whyWrong.B: Reverses cause and effect: the liquidity crises produced the defaults, not the other way around.
whyWrong.C: Hoffman and Norberg's work is named as something this research builds on; no errors in it are identified or corrected.
whyWrong.D: Hoffman and Norberg studied the link between state finance and political development, and the text never attributes any hypothesis about Philip's defaults to them.

tips: In a text that names prior work and then says "But their unique contribution is," the value being asked about lives entirely after the "But."

whyCorrect: The passage has two linked halves: specialization to a narrow Hawaiian habitat, and the vulnerability that specialization creates when the ecosystem is disturbed. A main idea has to carry the "However" as well as the setup, so it must include both the specialization and the resulting susceptibility.

whyWrong.A: Says the bird shares its habitat with no other species, which the text never claims — other Hawaiian birds are mentioned as similarly specialized.
whyWrong.B: Stops at the specialization and relatedness and leaves out the vulnerability the second sentence is devoted to.
whyWrong.D: Generalizes to all Hawaiian birds and turns the passage into a claim about where they can live, dropping the Kaua'i 'amakihi and the risk entirely.

commonMistakes: Choosing the option that covers only the first sentence when a "However" makes the second sentence the point.

whyCorrect: The claim needs figurative language that ties the two places together in one image. The line about the south wind carrying "soil of my homeland" to fall "like a fertile shower upon the lean streets" of Washington does exactly that: the rural South's soil is imagined reaching the city's streets, and "like a fertile shower" is the simile that makes it figurative.

whyWrong.A: Uses figurative language — whistles as "gasps and sobs," as "crude music" — but stays entirely within one setting and links no two places.
whyWrong.B: Describes the narrator singing; there is no image joining city and countryside.
whyWrong.C: Describes trees on V Street literally, with no figurative comparison and no reference to the South.

tips: For a claim about connecting two things, check that the quotation contains both of them, not just vivid language.

whyCorrect: The researchers' explanation is a chain: items in new locations make shoppers cover more of the store, they see more products, and they buy something unplanned. The shopper who could not find the cleaning supplies in their usual place, searched, spotted a notebook, and bought it too runs through every link of that chain.

whyWrong.B: Ends in items not found and nothing extra purchased, so the chain breaks before the unplanned purchase.
whyWrong.C: The extra purchase comes from a coupon, which is an obvious external cue, not the store's layout.
whyWrong.D: Attributes the trip to the store's size and selection, and the purchases were planned in advance.

tips: When an explanation is a chain of steps, the best evidence walks through all of them, not just the outcome.

whyCorrect: The conclusion is that mixing between lithosphere and mantle began 3.2 billion years ago. Direct support is evidence that mantle rock started containing lithospheric material at that point and not before. Mantle-derived rocks younger than 3.2 billion years carrying material absent from older mantle rocks but present in older lithospheric rocks is exactly that signature of mixing switching on.

whyWrong.A: Compares diversity within rocks that all predate the transition, which says nothing about when mixing began.
whyWrong.B: Runs the wrong way — it makes the oldest lithospheric rocks the most mantle-like, whereas mixing starting 3.2 billion years ago predicts greater similarity in the younger rocks.
whyWrong.C: Reports how many rocks of each type have been found, which reflects preservation and sampling, not chemical mixing.

tips: For a dating conclusion, the supporting finding must show the signature appearing on one side of the date and absent on the other.
